extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, press agents, advertisers, and students of public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations counselors on how to present ideas and influence public opinion by selecting media, segmenting publics, leveraging psychology and changed conditions, and constructing appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limits of PR over public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel is not responsible for creating or wholly controlling public opinion; the public’s established points of view are set by satisfying real or assumed human needs and the public itself influences leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume you can standardize or force uniform beliefs. Examples: Admiral Dewey alienated public affection despite counsel; Napoleon succeeded only when leading in the direction the public was already headed. Anti-pattern: Claiming PR can fully manufacture lasting public conviction irrespective of underlying needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use knowledge of individual and group psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: The counsel must constantly call upon knowledge of individual and group psychology to understand how opinions form and interact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step out of your own group to view problems impartially and use psychological insight to project the client’s point of view. This includes understanding herd reactions, ‘logic-proof compartments,’ and how individual minds aggregate into group minds. Practical application: analyze group allegiances, emotions, and impulses before crafting messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilize established mediums of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Proponents must work through existing channels (daily press, magazines, lecture circuits, advertising, motion pictures, radio, etc.) because innovators cannot feasibly create entirely new mass channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess which established medium best reaches each target subgroup. Consider cost, reach, and the audience’s expectations for freshness and quality of content. Anti-pattern: attempting to build/newspaper/radio/film distribution from scratch without enormous resources; overreliance on creating independent organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivide the public and tailor approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel must subdivide the appeal of his subject and present it through a variety of avenues adapted to different subgroups (majorities and minorities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze publics by demographics, occupations, interests, traditions, and languages; design distinct appeals for each segment. Example: Federation fundraising subdivided into dentists, bankers, real-estate operators, etc., each appealed to on its strongest group interest. Scoring note: campaigns that fail to segment will waste reach and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit interlapping group formations
rubrics_metrics.description: Society consists of many overlapping groups; the counsel should use these interlaps to reach individuals through multiple group identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map overlapping memberships (e.g., a person may be a music lover, motorist, banker). Craft messages that appeal to different group identities so the same individual encounters multiple complementary appeals. Example: Russian Ballet reached art lovers, music lovers, and society groups through different channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple, overlapping appeals to the same individual
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals respond when they encounter an idea framed in different ways tied to different aspects of their identity or interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure campaign touches target individuals via several appeals (e.g., fashion for women’s clubs, art for museum-goers, education for schools). This redundancy across identities increases acceptance; anti-pattern: single-line appeals expecting universal resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize on fundamental instincts and emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Extract ideas from the client’s cause that will capitalize on universal instincts (self-preservation, sex, hunger) and primary emotions (flight/fear, curiosity, pugnacity, parental love, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the instinct/emotion most relevant to the message (e.g., fear for public-health campaigns, curiosity for pre-announcement publicity, pugnacity to create combat/issue). Examples: heating ads appeal to shelter; food ads to gustatory sense; Woodbury’s to sex/attraction. Anti-pattern: ignoring emotional levers and relying solely on dry facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage changed external conditions and new media
rubrics_metrics.description: Changed physical or technological conditions (radio, automobile, airplane, inflation, strikes) alter group interests and receptivity; the counsel must account for and exploit these changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate how a new medium or condition changes viewpoints in specific publics and either enlarge the medium’s field for the client or interpret the change in terms favorable to the client’s interests. Example: use radio to reach farmers who are now more connected to world events. Scoring note: failure to recognize changed conditions reduces campaign effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize education/information rather than force or patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Among methods of securing cohesion, the public relations counsel avails himself primarily of education by information (third method) rather than patronage/pork or government by terror and obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor persuasive information campaigns that build self-consciousness and shared understanding (e.g., Committee on Public Information during war) while recognizing other methods may be used by states. Anti-pattern: relying on coercion or corrupt inducements as the principal PR strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek the greatest common factor to secure unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity in a heterogeneous public can be obtained only by finding broad, simple appeals (greatest common factor) that resonate across groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use universal themes such as loyalty, fairness, patriotism, or thrift to build consensus (example: railroad safety posters, appeals to employers and returned soldiers). Design messaging that abstracts to broad social/industrial purposes when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcome the ‘censorship’ of the group mind and herd reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda must be a directed effort to overcome the internal censorship of individuals and the herd reaction that blocks perception of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that audiences filter facts through preexisting absolutisms and logic-proof compartments; craft messages and channels to bypass or counter those filters (use feelers, curiosity-arousing devices, or trusted intermediaries). Practical tactic: present information through familiar, trusted channels and frames to reduce rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advise on form of action first, then select mediums
rubrics_metrics.description: The expert must first recommend the proper form of action for the client’s objective, and secondly utilize the established mediums best suited to present that action to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do strategic planning before media buying—determine whether the goal is information, agitation, sympathy, or behavior change, then choose channels and appeals aligned with that form. Anti-pattern: media-first approaches that lack a coherent action plan.
